entries.label: Short-run elasticity of R&D to its user cost
entries.units: elasticity (Δln R&D per Δln R&D user cost)

citation.authors: Nick Bloom, Rachel Griffith and John Van Reenen
citation.title: Do R&D tax credits work? Evidence from a panel of countries 1979–1997
citation.version: Abstract on the LSE Research Online record; DOI 10.1016/S0047-2727(01)00086-X

entries.quote: We estimate that a 10% fall in the cost of R&D stimulates just over a 1% rise in the level of R&D in the short-run, and just under a 10% rise in R&D in the long-run.
entries.derivation: Value = "just over a 1% rise" per 10% fall, taken as −0.1. The abstract gives no interval, so the range is the tool's ±50% rule (F-U-02).
entries.notes: Read in the abstract only ([A]); no full text could be reached (the LSE record has none and the SIEPR working-paper copy did not download). Panel of tax changes with country fixed effects.

entries.quote: We estimate that a 10% fall in the cost of R&D stimulates just over a 1% rise in the level of R&D in the short-run, and just under a 10% rise in R&D in the long-run.
entries.derivation: Value = "just under a 10% rise" per 10% fall, taken as −1.0. Range = the tool's ±50% rule (F-U-02).
entries.notes: Read in the abstract only ([A]). Australian additionality estimates for the R&D Tax Incentive (Holt, Skali and Thomson 2016; Swinburne) were seen only in secondary coverage and are not in the library.

entries.label: Long-run effect of business R&D (share of GDP) on (Harrod-neutral) multifactor productivity
entries.units: change in ln MFP per percentage point of GDP of business R&D funded by industry

citation.title: The quantification of structural reforms in OECD countries: A new framework
citation.publisher: OECD Economics Department Working Papers No. 1354, ECO/WKP(2016)78
citation.locator: Table 1, row 'business exp. On R&D by industry', columns (1)–(3), p. 10 (PDF p. 11); Table 4, row 'R&D (business exp.) (perc. of GDP)', p. 19 (PDF p. 20)

entries.quote: business exp. On R&D by industry 0.071** 0.059** 0.047** … R&D (business exp.) (perc. of GDP) 0.10 0.09% 0.17% 0.46%
entries.derivation: Value = column (3), the simulation column (0.047): +0.10 pp of GDP gives +0.47%, which Table 4 reports as +0.46% of GDP per head in the long run. Low and high = columns (3) and (1) (0.047 and 0.071).
entries.notes: Harrod-neutral MFP, so the long-run effect on GDP per head equals the MFP effect with K/Y fixed; enter it as labour-augmenting (A-P18). The paper itself calls the R&D effect small (p. 16). The 5- and 10-year effects (0.09%, 0.17%) are much slower than the long run.
